Stated Claim / Post Context:
Why do Gen Z watch TV with subtitles on? Youngsters reveal why they can't do without them - from fear of missing a crucial line to deciphering strong accents

YouGov quizzed subtitle-fans on their reasoning - and uncovered several key themes.

Actual Article Body:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR

Published:  21:21 AEDT, 27 October 2026   |  Updated:  01:50 AEDT, 28 October 2026

They are intended for the hard of hearing – and perhaps those of us who are getting on in years.

So many of a certain vintage will have been puzzled by why younger generations insist on watching TV with the subtitles on.

A YouGov study has found that the captions are more popular with Gen Z viewers than with any other age group.

More than half of those aged 18 to 24 (53 per cent) watched shows and films with the subtitles, compared with just 20 per cent of those aged 55 to 64, and 31 per cent of over-75s.

The survey of 35,753 Britons also asked the reasons why – with the explanations ranging from mumbling actors to struggling to follow unfamiliar accents.

The study authors added:  'A few gave other reasons for keeping subtitles on. These include keeping the volume down to avoid disturbing neighbours or sleeping children, and needing extra help to take in dialogue because of ADHD, autism or auditory processing difficulties.

'Others mention characters who talk too quickly, wanting to follow a programme while doing something else, such as looking at their phone or knitting, or living with someone who needs or wants subtitles on, such as a hard-of-hearing partner.'

Your browser does not support iframes.

YouGov's survey found that across all age groups, 30 per cent of Britons watch TV with subtitles on.

The researchers asked these viewers why they do so, with the answers overall fitting into six key explanations.

Some subtitle users said they find dialogue hard to hear, blaming poor sound mixing, loud music and a more naturalistic, mumbled style of acting.

'I often struggle to hear quieter dialogue or understand what's happening when multiple sounds overlap, so keeping the subtitles on is like safety barriers almost, ensuring I know what I should be hearing,' one young woman said.

Others say they see subtitles as a way of preventing the possibility of missing a crucial plot point, with one young man explaining: 'It means I don't miss anything and have a full understanding of what's going on without having to rewind.'

For others, subtitles have simply become the norm. 'It's become a habit for me to have them on. I feel strange without them!' one respondent said.

It's a question that puzzles many older Britons – why do Gen Z insist on watching TV with the subtitles on ?

Some find particular accents hard to follow, and say subtitles help them to understand dialogue they would otherwise struggle with.

Background noise from children, pets, or passing traffic was also a major theme.

One woman said: 'I have always lived in flats or house shares and don't want to disturb neighbours with loud TV.'

Meanwhile, some subtitle fans are simply hard of hearing, and describe subtitles as a necessity rather than a preference.

'I wear hearing aids so subtitles help and it means I don't have to raise the TV volume as much – although my wife is not hearing impaired, she will request that the subtitles are on a lot of the time,' one male respondent said.

The survey comes shortly after scientists claimed that parents should turn on TV subtitles to help their children learn to read.

Researchers found that children aged four to seven are twice as likely to become proficient readers if they watch TV with subtitles turned on.

And popular cartoons such as Peppa Pig and Bluey even contain a high number of 'high frequency words' that can help your child get ahead with their reading.

Henry Warren, co-founder of the Turn on the Subtitles campaign, said: 'I like to think of it a bit like sneaking vegetables into dinner – the children don't notice, but you know you're doing them the world of good.'
